title: How Elon Musk Really Makes His Money
the_thought: The big paycheck is a lock, not a deposit.
hook: A clerk slides a sheet across a table. The number on it is huge. About 158 billion dollars. Tesla put that number on Elon Musk's 2025 pay table. Then Tesla printed a second line for the same year. Realized pay: zero. The big paycheck is a lock, not a deposit. So who got paid?

levels.name: The Stub
beats: Watch the sheet the way a kid would. It sits in a filing room. It does not sit in a bank window. The boxes are simple. Salary. Bonus. Stock. Options. Total. For 2025 the salary box is empty. The bonus box is empty. The stock box is a mountain. The total is about 158 billion dollars. That is not a blog guess. That is Tesla's own pay table in a 2026 filing. Why print a number that big if nobody got the cash? Because the rule is not "money that landed in a bank." The rule is a picture of a gift on the day the gift is promised. Tesla says the picture and the real cash can be very different. But why keep both pictures on one sheet if only one of them is cash? So the first surprise is not "he is rich." The first surprise is this. The famous 2025 paycheck is a costume. The clerk did not hand him a box of bills. The clerk locked a stub. Break the 158 billion the simple way Tesla breaks it. About 132 billion is the picture of a new prize pack. About 26 billion is the picture of a short bridge pack. Add those two pictures and you get the table. So the huge total is two pictures glued together, not one pile of cash. That is adding. That is not a vibe. The bridge pack was later taken away. The table still had to show it. 2025 is when it was given. A lock that gets taken off the wall can still make last year's costume look fat. That is how the rule works. It is also why a person who only reads the total tells the wrong story. Tesla knew people would do that. Under the big table the company built a second table. Reported pay. Realized pay. Pay for a typical worker. Then a line Tesla named realized CEO pay. For 2025 that line is empty. Tesla treats it as zero. Next to a typical worker, the realized ratio is zero to one. Hold two ratios in one hand. Using the costume table, Tesla reports a pay ratio of more than two million to one. A typical qualifying worker is about 63 thousand dollars. Musk's reported total is about 158 billion. Using Tesla's own realized table, the ratio is zero. Same company. Same year. Same filing. Two answers. The person who bought a car in 2025 paid Tesla. Tesla's car sales that year were about 66 billion dollars. That money paid factories and batteries and chargers. It did not show up as a weekly wage on the CEO stub. The stub and the car lot are different machines. If you mix them, you will think lunch paid the lock. But the lunch ticket and the lock are not the same paper. So the mystery is not "is he wealthy." The mystery is a simple machine. If the table can print 158 billion, and the realized line can print zero, what paper can actually open? That question is the rest of the video. A reader who only sees the headline will treat the costume as a paycheck. That is why Tesla wrote a warning in the same filing. The camera clicks on the day the board stamps the gift. It does not wait for a share to unlock. It does not wait for a sale. It does not wait for tax. The number goes on the table. The lock can still sit in the cabinet. Why write the warning if the number is cash? Because the company already knows the next day's headlines will skip the footnote.

levels.name: The Zero Line
beats: Start with the simplest box: salary. Tesla says Musk once had a tiny base wage tied to California's minimum wage. Tesla also says he never took it. Starting in May 2019, at his request, Tesla stopped even writing that wage down. That is not a fan slogan. It is a footnote the company repeats. The empty 2025 salary box is not "we forgot." It is a rule that has been in force for years. There is no secret weekly Tesla paycheck hiding under the huge stock number. Why keep a zero wage if the table is going to scream? Because cash and locks do different jobs. Cash is a deposit. A lock is a reason to stay in the chair while the next gates are still shut. Tesla says most people get a wage plus stock. For the CEO, even the wage tool was removed. But why remove the wage if the stock picture is already huge? Because a wage would look like a deposit, and this board wanted a lock. Look at the rest of the named officers if you want a contrast the filing gives. Other bosses have a salary rate at year-end 2025. The CEO line does not. Tesla is not refusing to pay the factory. Tesla paid a typical qualifying worker about 63 thousand dollars. Tesla counted about 136 thousand people in that test at year-end 2025. About 43 percent of them were outside the United States. The factory gets a wage. The CEO stub gets a lock. That split is easy to miss if you only watch the huge ratio. More than two million to one is a real Tesla number. It is also a ratio But why does that change the lock? that uses the costume as the top. Swap the top for Tesla's realized zero and the factory wage is the only side that still has dollars. The typical worker did get paid. The CEO table did not. So the ratio is not a story about a plant that went unpaid. It is a story about two rulers glued to one cover page. The realized footnote is fussy on purpose. Tesla counts cash-like pay. It counts option cash only when shares were also sold, other than to cover taxes. For 2025 those boxes are empty. No salary. No bonus. No reported sale that fills the column. Zero is not a mood. Zero is the sum of empty boxes. That does not mean the man has no money life. It means this public company, in this year, did not record a realized But why does that change the lock? CEO payday on its extra table. Wealth can sit in a trust. A lock can sit unopened. A second company can sit on a second board. None of those facts turn the 158 billion into a deposit. People will still say he "made" 158 billion in 2025. The sentence is natural. It is also the sentence Tesla wrote a whole section to kill. The company says most of that figure is an accounting picture of the new prize pack. No shares from that pack have to have unlocked for the table to print. The gift date is enough. So why does the zero line matter for the title? Because "how he really makes his money" cannot start with a number the company itself refuses to call realized. The title is not "what a spreadsheet can print." The title is what opens.

levels.name: The Old Options
beats: The lock that already clicked open is older. But why does an old option matter if the 2025 table is the costume? Because this is the paper that can actually open. In January 2018 the Tesla board gave a long option. It covers about 304 million shares after later splits. The price stamp is about 23 dollars a share. The award was cut into 12 steps. Each step needed a company-size goal and a work goal. The first size step was 100 billion dollars. Later steps rose by 50 billion. Tesla now says all of the steps have been hit and checked by the board. All 12 parts have unlocked. He can use them if he pays the 23 dollar stamp, or uses a share-swap Tesla allows. That is the first real key on the Tesla side. Not a salary. A But why does that change the lock? price stamp. Do the multiplication if you want the cash hurdle, and keep it labeled as a hurdle. About 304 million times about 23 dollars is about 7 billion dollars if every option were paid in cash. Tesla also says he may swap shares instead, or mix cash and a swap. So 7 billion is the full cash price if he chose cash for every share. It is not a claim that he wrote that check. Why did a finished award still need a new deal in 2026? Because a court fight sat on top of it. Tesla names that fight in the filing. A higher Delaware court put the 2018 award back on December 19, 2025. The lower court wrote the final order on March 18, 2026. Only then could the company treat the award as fully usable again in the way the 2026 filing describes. But why add a new latch to a finished key? Because the court fight left a scar, and the board wanted him to stay in the job. On April 21, 2026 the board approved a new deal for using those options. Shares that come out take a job condition. Musk must stay as CEO, or in a product or operations job the independent directors approve, through January 19, 2028. Then a five-year hold starts. The lock opened. A new latch went on. That latch is easy to skip if you only want a victory lap. The options are unlocked. The court fight is over. And still the shares, once issued, can be taken back if the job condition fails. They also cannot be dumped the afternoon they appear. The hold is five years. But why does that change the lock? The title's answer is not "he cashed 2018." The answer is "he can use a finished lock, then stay in the chair, then wait." The ownership table already counts those option shares as if they were near his hand, because they could be used within 60 days of year-end 2025. Tesla's footnote is careful. Once issued under the new deal, the shares will be out and he may vote them. They still can be taken back if the job condition fails. A vote is not a sale. A vote is not a deposit. The trust is the other half of the owned pile. About 413 million shares sit in a family trust from 2003. Add the option shares and Tesla prints about 717 million shares, or 20.3 percent, using the year-end 2025 share count the footnote describes. That 20.3 percent But why does that change the lock? is the owned-and-near pile. It is not the 2025 prize pack. If you want a child-level picture of the old lock: a certificate with a 23 dollar stamp. The stamp is the toll. The court took the certificate away and then put it back. The new deal says you can use it if you keep the job through January 2028 and then wait five years to sell. That is how a finished option can still be a lock.

levels.name: The New Grant
beats: The 2025 costume is a different object. On September 3, 2025 the board granted about 424 million performance shares. Shareholders said yes on November 6, 2025. Tesla says the design copies the spirit of the 2018 award. The filing lists future size gates that run up to 8.5 trillion dollars, plus work gates on cars, software, bots, Robotaxis, and profit. Those work details matter because they are the combination on the lock. They do not matter as a promise that any gate has been hit. As of the April 30, 2026 filing, the 158 billion is still a gift-day picture. Tesla's realized table still shows a dash. The shares are not a 2025 deposit. One of those future gates already has a date on a different page. Tesla's 2025 report says the company started a Robotaxi service in June 2025, then ran it with Model Y cars. That is a product start, not an unlock notice. The pay filing still treats Robotaxis as a future work gate. A service can start and the lock can stay shut. Why mention the start at all? Because viewers will hear "Robotaxi" and assume the new pack already opened. The filing does not say that. It says the service started. The pack still needs its own gates. There is a second price hiding in the new pack. Any shares that unlock will be cut by about 334 dollars a share, unless he pays that cut in cash. The 2018 lock's toll is about 23 dollars. The 2025 lock's toll is about 334 dollars in share form, or cash if he chooses. Two different doors. Two different coins. Why approve a pack that large if the last one just survived a court? Tesla's special committee says that after the 2018 award was earned, the company lacked a next prize for the next phase. That is the board's public reason. This video does not have to agree that 8.5 trillion dollars is a wise target. It only has to say the target is how the new lock is cut. But the new pack is still a sealed case, not a 2025 deposit. The bridge pack was a third object, and it died. In August 2025 the board approved 96 million restricted shares, with the same 23 dollar stamp. Tesla says the point was to give voting power while the court still blocked the 2018 options, and to keep him in a leadership role for two years. The pack would be taken away if a final court order But why does that change the lock? let him use the 2018 award. On April 21, 2026 the independent directors said that event had happened. The bridge pack was taken away in full. So about 26 billion dollars of the 2025 table is a lock that was later taken off the wall. The table cannot unprint 2025. The cabinet can. That is another reason the costume and the cabinet disagree. The 424 million prize shares are also left out of the 20.3 percent ownership line. Tesla says they sit under a voting deal. A proxy goes to Tesla's secretary to vote those shares with the rest of the room, including Musk. He does not control those shares. A gift can be huge and still not count as "his pile" on the ownership table. That is not a riddle. That is the footnote. If the 2018 certificate is But why does that change the lock? a key with a 23 dollar stamp, the 2025 pack is a sealed case with a 334 dollar stamp and a list of future gates. The clerk can assign it a 132 billion dollar picture on day one. The case can still be empty of spendable shares.

levels.name: The Other Ticker
beats: Tesla is not the only public board in the room anymore. But why open a second set of books if the Tesla stub already printed 158 billion? Because a founder's pile can sit on more than one board, and Tesla's realized line still does not explain SpaceX. SpaceX now files as a public company. Its stock trades as SPCX. The mid-2026 report is a second set of books that did not exist for a long video a year earlier. So the lock story has to leave the car lot. For the quarter ended June 30, 2026 SpaceX reported about 7.8 billion dollars of sales, up from about 4.1 billion a year earlier. For six months, about 12.5 billion versus about 8.1 billion. The mix is not "rockets only." Space was about 962 million in the quarter. The dish business was about But why does that change the lock? 4.3 billion. The AI piece was about 2.6 billion. The dish is louder than the launch pad on that particular sheet. SpaceX's August 4, 2026 earnings note reported a quarterly loss of 541 million dollars, better than a 1 billion dollar loss a year earlier. A second board can grow sales and still lose money. That is allowed. It is also a warning against treating a founder's stake as a weekly paycheck. The company can miss a profit and the ownership percent can still sit there. How did X and xAI get inside that board? The report is blunt. On February 2, 2026 SpaceX bought xAI. Before that, on March 28, 2025, xAI bought the X companies. Twitter was bought by Elon Musk in October 2022. The public company now carries launch, dishes, and an AI piece that did not start as a rocket part. Do not turn that history into a private-chat fortune number. The filing gives dates and boxes. It does not hand this video a single "Musk net worth" that can be spoken as fact. What it does hand over is an August 13, 2026 ownership form: about 6.4 billion SpaceX shares on a converted basis, 48.4 percent of that class. The percent uses the mid-2026 share count plus the extra shares the form adds into the math. Inside that 48.4 percent are four different objects. Trust Class A shares. Trust Class B shares. Restricted Class B shares he may vote, still tied to performance. And options on Class B. Some of that pile is a lock too. Restricted stock that still has gates is not a deposit. Class B can turn into Class A. Class A But why does that change the lock? has one vote. Class B has ten votes. That is the rule in the report and in the ownership form. The form does not print one voting-power percent on the cover. So this video will not invent 80 percent, or 82 percent, or any other upgrade. It will say what the papers say: ten votes on Class B, one vote on Class A, and a 48.4 percent converted Class A claim. The share counts themselves were restated. In May 2026 SpaceX split the stock five-for-one. The mid-2026 report says older share figures were rolled forward so they match the new count. If an older article quotes a smaller pile, it may be talking about the pre-split paper. This cut stays on the split-adjusted report and the August form. Why put SpaceX in a Tesla-pay video? Because the title is how he makes his money, not how one car company makes its money. Tesla's 2025 realized CEO line is zero. SpaceX is a second public pile with its own locks. If you only watch the 158 billion stub, you will miss the dish, the launch, and the restricted Class B. The person who pays for a dish is still not writing a founder wage. That person pays SpaceX. SpaceX reports the sale. The founder's form is an ownership claim, not a receipt from that person.

levels.name: What He Can Borrow
beats: If the stubs are locks, how does anyone buy groceries? The honest public answer is smaller than the gossip. Tesla shows a pledge rule and a count of shares that may stand behind a loan. It does not hand this video a monthly personal budget. At year-end 2025 the ownership footnote includes about 207 million Tesla shares that may be pledged. Eligible is not the same as borrowed. Tesla also says that, based on written statements, the actual officer-and-director borrowing against pledged shares was under 1 percent of the pledged value at that year-end. But why print a 3.5 billion dollar lid if the last snapshot of actual use was tiny? Because a lid is a rule, not a receipt. The board rule is a lid, not a withdrawal slip. For the CEO, the loan against pledged stock may not exceed 3.5 billion dollars, or a quarter of the pledged pile, whichever is smaller. Tesla notes that pledging does not tell you how much was actually borrowed. Actual borrowing may be much less than the value of the shares pledged. So the public machine for "cash now" is a window with a lid. The lid is 3.5 billion or a quarter of the pledged pile. The last snapshot of actual officer-and-director use was tiny next to the pledged value. That is the opposite of a secret unlimited cash machine. It is also not proof that any one night's dinner was paid a particular way. The 2025 prize pack and the 2018 deal, Tesla says, allow the CEO to pledge shares from those packs to sell in an orderly way. That sentence is about permission. It is not a 2025 sale ticket. Why mention borrowing at all? Because viewers will ask the cash question, and the filing actually answers a version of it. The answer is not "he takes a salary." The answer is "some owned shares may stand behind loans, under a published lid, and the last snapshot of actual borrowing was tiny." If a later filing changes the pledged count, that would be a new period. This video stays on the April 30, 2026 Tesla amendment and the year-end 2025 table. No invented loan balance. No invented interest rate. Why is the window so small next to the costume? Because a pledged share is still a share he already owns, not a new gift. The 158 billion line is a picture of unopened paper. The pledge footnote is a picture of owned paper that may stand behind a loan. Mixing those two pictures is how a viewer ends up saying Tesla "paid" him last year when the realized box is empty. The filing keeps them on different pages for a reason.

levels.name: Why The Lock Exists
beats: The strange decision that makes sense is this. Tesla would rather print a 158 billion dollar costume than write a cash bonus that lands. SpaceX would rather report a 48.4 percent converted stake with restricted shares still inside it than describe a weekly founder wage. The lock is not a glitch in the paperwork. The lock is the product the boards bought. Tesla's text is almost proud of the gap. Stock is how you keep someone through a long mission. The 2018 award paid off, in the company's telling, because the size steps and the work steps were hit. The 2025 award is the sequel. The bridge pack was a bridge during a court fight, then it was removed when the old lock came back. Each object has a job. None of the jobs is "deposit 158 billion in 2025." Look But why does that change the lock? at Tesla's year if you want the other side of the table. Total sales were about 95 billion dollars in fiscal 2025, down from about 98 billion. Car sales fell 9 percent to about 66 billion. Energy storage rose 27 percent to about 13 billion. Profit for common stockholders was about 3.8 billion, down from about 7.1 billion. The car company made a profit. The profit is not the CEO's wage. 3.8 billion of profit cannot be a 158 billion cash paycheck. The arithmetic refuses. But why would a down year in cars still print a fat costume? Because the costume is not a slice of car sales. The mix inside that year also refuses the simple car-salary story. Car sales shrank. Energy grew. The pay table still screamed. If lunch at the lot paid the lock, a down year in car sales should have shrunk the stub. It did not, because the stub is not a slice of car sales. It is a gift-day photograph of future gates. So a viewer who wants "how the cars pay him" is asking the wrong counter. The cars pay Tesla. Tesla's profit is about 3.8 billion. The costume is larger than that profit. It is not a slice of it. That is not a bonus formula. That is a pricing model sitting on a different desk. SpaceX's quarter makes the same point from the other direction. The dish can be 4.3 billion dollars in three months. The company can still post a 541 million dollar loss. An AI piece can print 2.6 billion of sales and still sit inside a losing whole. Ownership percents do not deposit themselves into a personal account But why does that change the lock? because a piece grew. The weakness belongs next to the strength or the video starts cheering. Tesla car sales are down. Tesla profit is down. The 2025 prize shares are unearned. The 2018 shares, once issued, can still be taken back if the job breaks before January 19, 2028. SpaceX can lose money. Restricted SpaceX Class B still has gates. Pledging is capped. A lock can fail to open. A lock can open and still not be cash if a hold sits on top. There is also a rules weakness Tesla already lived. A court took the 2018 award away before another court put it back. That is not a cartoon villain scene. It is a reminder that a lock sitting in Delaware can freeze a finished option. The 2026 deal is the scar. Why do boards keep building locks anyway? Because a cash wage would be small next to the stock pile and would not, in their stated view, buy the same years of attention. That is their filing voice. This video does not have to clap for the next target. It only has to say the target is how the new lock is cut.

levels.name: Who Opens It
beats: So how does Elon Musk really make his money? Not by a Tesla salary. Tesla stopped writing one down in May 2019, and he had not been taking it before that. Not by taking the 158 billion dollar table home in 2025. Tesla's own realized line for that year is zero. The big paycheck is a lock, not a deposit. The Tesla pile that can open is older paper: about 304 million options at about 23 dollars, finished, now wrapped in a job latch through January 19, 2028 and a five-year hold. The Tesla pile that cannot yet open is newer paper: about 424 million prize shares with a 334 dollar cut and a list of future gates, plus a voting deal that keeps them out of the 20.3 percent line. The Tesla pile that is already his is the trust: But why does that change the lock? about 413 million shares. Together with the option shares, Tesla calls that 20.3 percent. The SpaceX pile is a second board. 48.4 percent on a converted Class A method, including restricted shares that still have gates. Mid-2026 quarterly sales were about 7.8 billion dollars. That is the company's sales, not his wage. The cash window the filing will admit is a pledge lid and a year-end snapshot that says actual officer-and-director borrowing was under 1 percent of pledged value. Eligible Tesla shares in the footnote: about 207 million. Lid for the CEO: 3.5 billion dollars or a quarter of pledged value, whichever is smaller. If you remember one pair of numbers after the credits, remember 158 billion and zero, fiscal 2025, same Tesla filing, reported versus realized. If you remember one object, remember the padlock on the stub. If you But why does that change the lock? remember one customer, remember that the buyer paid the car company. The car company printed a lock. A company-level SpaceX video would have to explain a different invoice: a dish that already outruns launch, an AI piece that arrived by merger, and a quarter that can grow fast and still lose 541 million dollars. That is a different title. This one ends on the stub.

A company that sells dishes and launches, and now files as a public board of its own, would have to explain how the dish pays the pad. That title is waiting if this one holds. But why split the founder lock from the company invoice? Because the dish is a different counter.
